tagline.text: A remote island at Quezon's far east edge, with golden sand and Pacific cliffs

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱3,800–4,500 (2 nights/3 days from Manila, per person)

children.text: Jomalig is the smallest and least populated island municipality in Quezon, with golden-sand beaches facing the Pacific and a grass-covered cliff viewpoint. It takes 9–11 hours each way from Manila, so this is an adventure destination that needs preparation.
Jomalig is an island municipality at the eastern end of Quezon, facing the open Philippine Sea and the Pacific Ocean. It lies about
139 km

(75 nautical miles) southeast of the Polillo Islands and is made up of five barangays: Apad, Bukal, Casuguran, Gango and Talisoy. With about 7,900 residents in the 2024 census, it is the least populated municipality in the province, and most people live off coconut, rice, fishing and root crops. It became a municipality on June 18, 1961 under Republic Act No. 3372.

What makes the island known among travelers is the color of its sand. At beaches such as Salibungot, quartz grains coated with iron make the sand look deep gold or orange, and long rows of agoho (Casuarina) pines line the shore. The west side has relatively calm beaches, while the east has rough, wave-battered rocky coast and grass-covered cliffs, so one island offers very different scenery.

Getting there is not easy, though. There is no airport and no RoRo terminal. From Ungos Port in Real on the mainland, you ride a wooden outrigger boat (banca) that mainly carries cargo and cross the sea for about
5–6 hours

. Departure can slip until the cargo is full, and in rough-sea seasons boats do not sail at all. Lodging is in simple huts, electricity runs only a few hours a day, and there is no Wi-Fi. It suits travelers who want a raw island atmosphere rather than comfort.

This guide is based on trip reports from September 2026 and 2026 municipal information about Jomalig. Boat schedules, fares and entrance fees change often with local conditions, so check the latest information before you leave.

This is the island's signature beach, with deep golden sand and a pine grove of agoho trees. At low tide a wide sandbar appears, which is great for walks and photos. Pacific waves are strong and rip currents occur, so treat it as a place to walk rather than swim.
With fine white sand and shallow, calm water, this is the safest place on the island to swim. Entrance costs about
, and the beach is short, so it can get crowded on weekends.

blocks.title: Kanaway Beach and the "Tree of No Forever"

children.text: This stretch of the east coast has layered rock formations and tidal pools. A lone dapdap tree bent by the Pacific wind is the most photographed sight on the island. The seabed is sharp rock and the swells are unpredictable, so it is best not to swim here.
The nickname comes from grass-covered hills dropping to vertical cliffs, a scene that resembles Batanes. It is most beautiful in the late afternoon as the sun sinks. Entrance costs about
, and you cannot swim here.

A motorized bangka takes you around Manlanat Islet (bouldering and birdwatching), Canaway Islet (turtle-shaped rocks visible at low tide) and the sandbars off Sitio Pitisan. There is no booking office, so it is common to ask your resort host the day before.
With no paved roads on the island, you tour it by motorcycle taxi (habal-habal) modified for sand. The driver doubles as a guide, and a full-day circuit costs about
according to trip reports. It is easy to get lost on the sandy paths, so travel with a local driver.
Resort cooks prepare fish and shellfish that fishermen caught that day. There is no menu; you pay for the catch plus a cooking fee (about
per person, varying by resort; check whether rice and water are included), which is reported as a common practice on the island.

Power usually cuts out around 1 AM and there is little artificial light, so the night sky is dark. Sunsets on the western beaches are also lovely, so on the first day we suggest taking it easy and resting at the beach.

items.title: Standard 2-night, 3-day plan
items.subtitle: The minimum schedule given the long travel

children.text: Take the late-night bus to Real from the Legarda Street terminal in Sampaloc, Manila.
Get off at the Real highway, take a tricycle to Ungos Port, and at the small office at the entrance write your name on the Coast Guard passenger list and pay the fees.
The boat leaves once it is loaded with cargo. You will spend about 5–6 hours in the hot sun, so prepare motion sickness medicine and a dry bag.
Pay the environmental and tourism fee at Talisoy and head to your lodging. On the first day, rest and watch the sunset from a nearby beach.
On a habal-habal circuit, visit Salibungot, Kanaway and Lingayen Cove in turn, and enjoy the view at Lingayen Cove in the late afternoon.
Trip reports say return boats leave early on weekdays and late in the morning on weekends. Confirm the time at your lodging the day before.
Total travel time is about 9–11 hours each way. A weekend-only trip is possible but very tight, so we recommend three days or more.

items.title: Plan with island hopping
items.subtitle: One more day if the boats can run

children.text: Book a small bangka (4–6 people) through your lodging and head out to Manlanat Islet and Canaway Islet.
Have lunch on the sandbar off Sitio Pitisan.
Return, then swim and relax at Little Boracay beach.
Trip reports mention about ₱1,200 for a small bangka and ₱4,000 or more for a large boat, so it is best to split the cost with your group.

The one-way fare is about

At low tide the boat cannot reach the beach, so you cross the last
on a bamboo raft (balsa) for about

Some guides say waves are too high for sailing from October to mid-March because of the northeast monsoon (amihan). Plan your trip for a good-weather period between November and May.
The island has no paved coastal road, jeepneys or standard tricycles. Motorcycle taxis (habal-habal) are the main transport.

Sea conditions decide whether you can travel to Jomalig. Trip reports say November to May is relatively better, and March to May is the driest and most reliable. This is peak season, so it is safer to book lodging 3–4 weeks ahead.

June to October is southwest monsoon and typhoon season. When PAGASA issues a gale warning, the Coast Guard grounds all boats and you can be stranded for days. Some guides also say waves are high from October to mid-March because of the northeast monsoon, so always check the forecast just before departure.

The island has simple resorts and homestay-style lodging. Trip reports from 2026 mention South Pacific Island Resort (bahay kubo about
), Tejada's Resort (about
), El Vito Resort and Jojomalig Resort (nipa hut about
). Beach camping outside accredited resorts is banned by local ordinance, and without a booking drivers may not take you to the beach, so reserve ahead.
Electricity comes from a diesel plant, usually only in the evening, about
to

(some guides say it starts at 17:00 or runs into the daytime, so confirm with your resort), and there is no Wi-Fi. You eat paluto-style at the resort, and since ATMs cannot be relied on, bring all your cash from Manila, mostly in small bills. Buy snacks at the Real market, and bring reusable containers because single-use plastic is restricted by ordinance.
The bus leaves late at night, so you board the boat without sleep. Take motion sickness medicine 30 minutes before boarding and keep your dry bag between your legs.
You will be in direct sun for over 5 hours on the boat. Bring a hat, sunscreen (SPF 50 or higher) and plenty of water.
Bring plenty of ₱20, ₱50 and ₱100 bills. Raft boatmen and motorcycle drivers have no change for large bills.
A power bank (16,000–20,000 mAh) is essential. Charging is usually available only in the evening until about 1 AM; hours vary, so ask your resort.
Skip the island tour on arrival day and do it on day two, since the first day's travel fatigue is heavy.
Water shoes are a must for coral and sharp rock. Also pack antihistamines and anti-diarrheal medicine.
Bring a headlamp for the blackout after 1 AM.
Trip reports say return boats leave early on weekdays and late in the morning on weekends. Leave slack in your return schedule.
There are no lifeguards at any beach and rip currents are strong. Night swimming is banned by local ordinance, and boats can be grounded for days during a weather warning.
Rip currents are strong at Salibungot and the eastern coves. If caught, swim parallel to the shore to escape.
Swells at Kanaway are unpredictable and the rocks are sharp, so do not swim there.
The island health center treats only minor wounds. Serious cases are taken by sea ambulance to Real or Infanta, reportedly for about ₱250, depending on the weather.
Jellyfish and sea lice are said to be more common from July to October. Avoid visiting then.
During weather warnings the Coast Guard grounds all boats, so leave slack in your return schedule.
A beach island in the same province of Quezon, good for mainland-side sea and white sand. It is also sometimes introduced in Jomalig guides as a place to visit together.
An island off the Quezon coast, much closer to Manila than Jomalig, so it suits a shorter trip.
A farm-style resort inland in Quezon that you can include in a Quezon itinerary.
A town famous for the Pahiyas Festival and its food culture. Trip-report guides suggest it as a place to see alongside a Jomalig trip.
